title: LLM Performance on CSLib-Style Problems vs. Mathlib-Style Problems: Is CS Verification Harder Than Math?

original_idea.body:
# LLM Performance on CSLib-Style Problems vs. Mathlib-Style Problems: Is CS Verification Harder Than Math?

**Problem:** CSLib targets computer science algorithms (sorting, searching, graphs); Mathlib targets pure mathematics (topology, algebra, number theory). Whether LLMs perform differently on CS-style vs. math-style Lean 4 problems — and why — is unknown.

**Direction:** Sample 30 CS-style problems (algorithm verification) and 30 math-style problems of similar proof length from Lean 4 benchmarks. Run the same LLMs on both sets. Measure compilation rate, proof success rate, and failure mode distribution. Test whether CS problems are systematically harder or easier.

**Why it matters:** CSLib is the primary target for safety-relevant formal verification. If CS-style proofs are harder than math-style proofs for LLMs, the safety applications of formal verification are harder than benchmark scores on Mathlib-derived tasks suggest.

**Relevant context:** Mathlib has the most Lean 4 training data. CSLib is newer and smaller. Whether models trained on Mathlib transfer to CS verification tasks is an important generalization question for the CSLib project.

title: Formal Verification Test Harness for AIxCC Finalist Systems: Measuring What Formal Methods Could Add

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification Test Harness for AIxCC Finalist Systems: Measuring What Formal Methods Could Add

**Problem:** AIxCC finalist systems used dynamic analysis and LLM semantic reasoning. Whether adding formal verification (Dafny/Lean precondition checking) to these systems would improve vulnerability detection in the competition infrastructure is untested.

**Direction:** Take the open-source AIxCC finalist systems (available after August 2025). Add a formal verification module (LLM-generated Dafny preconditions checked against each vulnerability candidate). Re-run on the competition challenge set. Measure whether formal verification adds any bugs to the 77% detection rate.

**Why it matters:** This experiment directly tests whether formal methods + AI is better than AI alone for vulnerability detection — the core claim of the RAND report. If it adds detection, the case for formal verification in security is empirically grounded.

**Relevant context:** AIxCC SoK paper (arXiv 2602.07666) analyzes all finalist systems. Open-source release planned for August 2025. RAND advocates formal methods + AI combination. No experiment tests this combination on the AIxCC infrastructure.

title: Formal Verification Interpretability: Can LLMs Explain Why a Lean 4 Proof Is Correct in Plain English?

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification Interpretability: Can LLMs Explain Why a Lean 4 Proof Is Correct in Plain English?

**Problem:** Lean 4 proofs are machine-checkable but often uninterpretable to non-experts. Whether LLMs can generate accurate natural language explanations of formal proofs — making them interpretable without loss of correctness — is untested.

**Direction:** Take 25 complete Lean 4 proofs of varying complexity. Ask LLMs to generate natural language explanations of each. Have Lean experts rate explanations for accuracy and completeness. Measure explanation accuracy vs. proof complexity. Test whether less complex proofs receive more accurate explanations.

**Why it matters:** Interpretable formal proofs are essential for human oversight of AI-generated verification. If proofs cannot be explained in plain language, human review is limited to checking compilation rather than understanding correctness.

**Relevant context:** Lean 4 has a REPL interface and proof state display. LLM explanation of code is studied in software engineering. Explanation of formal proofs specifically is not studied and has different requirements than code explanation.

title: Formal Verification of Role-Based Access Control: A Near-Term Security Deployment Target

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification of Role-Based Access Control: A Near-Term Security Deployment Target

**Problem:** Role-based access control (RBAC) policies have formal models (RBAC96). Whether LLMs can generate Lean 4 proofs that an access control implementation correctly implements a given RBAC policy is unstudied.

**Direction:** Model an RBAC policy in Lean 4 (users, roles, permissions, constraints). Write formal specs for RBAC safety properties (role containment, separation of duties). Generate implementations using LLMs. Attempt to prove conformance to the formal RBAC model. Measure success rate.

**Why it matters:** Access control failures cause major security breaches. Formally verified RBAC implementation would provide mathematical guarantees that authorization logic is correct. This is a tractable, high-value near-term formal verification target.

**Relevant context:** RBAC96 model is well-formalized in the literature. Lean 4 can express the RBAC model. No study has attempted LLM-generated Lean proofs of RBAC implementations. This is a concrete formal verification security application.

original_idea.body:
# Human Expert Vs. AI on Lean 4 Proof Time: Measuring the Human-AI Gap and Identifying Where AI Helps Most

**Problem:** No time comparison exists between expert humans and current AI (with/without AI assistance) on the same Lean 4 tasks. This gap analysis is fundamental for understanding where AI most accelerates formal verification.

**Direction:** Recruit 5 Lean 4 experts and 5 novices (CS students). Each solves 10 VeriBench tasks: (a) without AI assistance, (b) with Claude/Leanstral assistance. Measure time per task and success rate per condition. Compare to automated AI baseline (no human). Plot the human-AI collaboration efficiency frontier.

**Why it matters:** Understanding where human experts are still faster than AI, and where AI accelerates experts, is foundational for designing effective human-AI collaboration workflows for safety-critical formal verification.

**Relevant context:** No published study compares human expert and AI time on Lean 4 tasks. RAND calls for accelerating formal verification adoption. This user study would provide the empirical foundation for that recommendation.

title: Specification Mining from Lean Mathlib: Can LLMs Extract Safety-Relevant Specs from Existing Proofs?

original_idea.body:
# Specification Mining from Lean Mathlib: Can LLMs Extract Safety-Relevant Specs from Existing Proofs?

**Problem:** Lean's Mathlib contains thousands of formally proven theorems. Whether LLMs can mine these proofs to extract specification patterns relevant to security applications (boundedness, monotonicity, commutativity) is unstudied.

**Direction:** Sample 50 Mathlib theorems relevant to programming (sorting, arithmetic, data structures). Use LLMs to extract general specification patterns. Test whether these patterns transfer to new programs as starting specifications. Measure whether Mathlib-sourced specs lead to higher proof success rates than LLM-generated specs from scratch.

**Why it matters:** Mathlib is a vast, formally verified knowledge base. If it can be mined for reusable specification patterns, it provides a head start for security-critical formal verification without requiring new spec writing.

**Relevant context:** Mathlib has 100K+ theorems. CSLib will extend this to CS algorithms. Specification mining from Mathlib for new applications is not studied. This could significantly reduce spec writing overhead.

title: Formal Verification Coverage of OWASP Top 10: Which Web Vulnerabilities Can Lean 4 Address?

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification Coverage of OWASP Top 10: Which Web Vulnerabilities Can Lean 4 Address?

**Problem:** The OWASP Top 10 defines the most critical web security vulnerabilities. A systematic analysis of which OWASP Top 10 vulnerability classes can be formally specified and verified in Lean 4 has not been done.

**Direction:** For each of the OWASP Top 10 vulnerability classes, attempt to: (a) write a formal Lean 4 specification capturing vulnerability absence, (b) generate an LLM-assisted proof for a simple case. Classify each as: formally specifiable + provable, specifiable but not provable with current tools, or not formally specifiable.

**Why it matters:** A systematic coverage analysis of OWASP Top 10 by formal methods would define the scope of what formal verification can and cannot guarantee for web security. This provides practical guidance for security teams on where to apply formal methods.

**Relevant context:** OWASP Top 10 is the standard web security reference. RAND benchmarks mention injection, access control. No systematic mapping of OWASP vulnerabilities to formal verification coverage exists. This is a natural gap-filling study.

original_idea.body:
# Secure Proof Synthesis Benchmark: Evaluating AI on Combined Security + Formal Verification Tasks

**Problem:** No benchmark combines the two skills needed for Secure Program Synthesis (SPS): (1) generating secure code and (2) formally verifying security properties. Current benchmarks test each skill separately.

**Direction:** Create a 50-task benchmark where each task requires: (a) generating code that passes security review criteria AND (b) providing a formal Lean 4 proof of a security property. Measure LLM performance on the combined task vs. each sub-task independently. Test whether solving both simultaneously degrades performance on each.

**Why it matters:** SPS is identified as a major 2026 focus in the subfield context. A benchmark for combined security+verification capability would directly measure progress on this joint capability. It would also reveal whether there are tradeoffs between the two skills.

**Relevant context:** VeriBench measures formal verification. AIxCC and Claude Code Security measure vulnerability detection. No benchmark requires demonstrating both simultaneously. SPS as a concept needs a dedicated evaluation framework.

title: Compounding Risk: Sorry-Using Proofs × Production Deployment = Undetected Incomplete Verification

original_idea.body:
# Compounding Risk: Sorry-Using Proofs × Production Deployment = Undetected Incomplete Verification

**Problem:** If Lean 4 proofs using 'sorry' (a placeholder that makes any goal provable) are deployed in production without sorry detection, developers believe they have formal guarantees they do not have. This compounding risk of sorry usage + deployment without sorry checking is not characterized.

**Direction:** Survey open-source Lean 4 code on GitHub. Measure frequency of sorry usage in non-research, non-draft code. Survey developers on whether they check for sorry before deployment. Design and test a simple CI/CD sorry-detection tool. Measure developer awareness of the sorry failure mode.

**Why it matters:** If production Lean 4 code contains sorry placeholders that developers believe are complete proofs, formal verification provides false safety guarantees at scale. This is a practical deployment failure mode that urgently needs characterization.

**Relevant context:** Sorry is documented as a proof debt mechanism in the Lean community. Production sorry usage outside of research is not measured. No CI/CD sorry-detection tool is mentioned in any formal verification deployment paper.

title: Multi-Agent Formal Verification: Does a Debate-Style Protocol Between Two LLM Verifiers Improve Proof Quality?

original_idea.body:
# Multi-Agent Formal Verification: Does a Debate-Style Protocol Between Two LLM Verifiers Improve Proof Quality?

**Problem:** When one LLM generates a Lean 4 proof and another LLM critiques it (debate protocol), the combination may catch more errors than single-LLM generation. Whether multi-agent debate improves Lean 4 proof quality is untested.

**Direction:** Implement a two-agent protocol: LLM A generates a Lean 4 proof, LLM B critiques it (identifies potential errors), LLM A revises. Compare compilation rate and proof quality (vacuity rate, mutation survival) between: (a) single-agent, (b) two-agent debate, (c) two independent single-agents choosing the better output.

**Why it matters:** Multi-agent debate is proposed as a scalable oversight method in AI safety. Testing it specifically in formal verification provides empirical evidence for whether debate protocols improve correctness in machine-checkable domains.

**Relevant context:** Multi-agent debate (Irving et al.) is an AI safety proposal. Claude Code Security uses multi-stage verification (single agent). Whether two different models in debate mode improves formal verification quality is not tested.

**Direction:** Ask 3 LLMs to generate Python/Rust implementations of AES-256, SHA-256, and RSA key generation. **Relevant context:** RAND (2026) lists cryptographic implementation verification as a benchmark target. EverCrypt and HACL* are examples of formally verified cryptographic libraries. AI-generated crypto code is specifically not yet validated through formal methods.

title: Formal Verification of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: Can Lean 4 Check LLM Reasoning Steps?

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: Can Lean 4 Check LLM Reasoning Steps?

**Problem:** LLM chain-of-thought reasoning produces informal mathematical arguments. Whether formal verification tools can check the correctness of LLM mathematical reasoning steps (treating CoT as a formal proof sketch) is unexplored.

**Direction:** Take 20 LLM chain-of-thought solutions to mathematical problems. Attempt to formalize each CoT step as a Lean 4 tactic sequence. Measure: (a) what fraction of CoT solutions are faithfully formalizable, (b) what fraction of formalized proofs compile without error, (c) where CoT reasoning is formally incorrect.

title: Formal Verification of OAuth/OIDC Flow: Can AI Generate Correct Protocol Security Proofs?

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification of OAuth/OIDC Flow: Can AI Generate Correct Protocol Security Proofs?

**Problem:** OAuth 2.0 and OIDC are widely used authentication protocols with known formal security models. Whether LLMs can generate Lean 4 or ProVerif proofs that an implementation correctly implements these protocols is untested.

**Direction:** Select a simple OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow implementation. Write formal ProVerif/Lean 4 specs for: (a) token secrecy, (b) authentication guarantee, (c) CSRF prevention. Ask LLMs to generate proofs. Measure success rate. Compare to known human-written ProVerif models of OAuth.

**Why it matters:** Authentication protocols are the most critical security layer in web applications. Formally verified OAuth implementations would provide mathematical guarantees against token theft and impersonation attacks.

**Relevant context:** ProVerif has been used to find flaws in OAuth (Fett et al. 2016). Lean 4 can also model protocols. LLM-generated protocol security proofs have not been tested on real-world protocols like OAuth.

Identifying which specific application domains (safety-critical embedded systems, cryptographic libraries, policy enforcement code) have the highest benefit-cost ratio for formal verification is not done.

**Direction:** Build a structured 2x2 analysis: x-axis = AI code generation rate, y-axis = formal verification current capability. Plot 20 application domains on this grid. Identify high-AI-use + high-verifiability quadrant as ideal early adopters. Survey 10 developers in each candidate domain on deployment readiness.

**Why it matters:** Targeted deployment in high-value domains would generate evidence for broader adoption while managing risk. Without identifying early adopter use cases, formal verification for AI-generated code may stall in research without impacting production.

**Relevant context:** RAND calls for broad adoption but does not prioritize specific use cases. Technology adoption curves suggest starting with early adopters. This strategic analysis would provide the evidence base for policy recommendations on where to invest.
